definition: FreeHAL was a volunteer computing project to build a self-learning chatbot.
details: This project is no longer active. Originally, the program was called JEliza referring to the chatbot ELIZA by Joseph Weizenbaum. The J stood for Java because JEliza has first been programmed in Java. In May 2008, the program has been renamed to FreeHAL because the programming language has changed. The name is related to the computer in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey. FreeHAL uses a semantic network and technologies like pattern recognition, stemming, part of speech databases and Hidden Markov Models in order to imitate a human behaviour. FreeHAL learns autonomously. While communicating by keyboard, the program extends its database. Currently, English and German are supported. By using the BOINC platform, new semantic networks for the program are built. FreeHAL@home appears to have terminated operations.

explainer.lead: FreeHAL was an experiment in letting a chatbot teach itself through ordinary typed conversations, with volunteers' computers helping build its knowledge. It combined language-processing techniques with a semantic network and is no longer active.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a chatbot with a notebook that grows every time someone talks to it. FreeHAL tried to turn typed conversations into useful knowledge, while volunteers lent computer power to help build bigger knowledge maps. It could chat in English and German, but the project has now stopped.
tiers.practitioner: For an engineer, FreeHAL is a historical example of combining dialogue-driven learning with distributed computing. Its pipeline used pattern recognition, stemming, part-of-speech databases and Hidden Markov Models to update a semantic network, while BOINC supported the construction of new networks. It should not be treated as a currently maintained system: development covered English and German, and FreeHAL@home has terminated operations.
tiers.paperLevel: FreeHAL can be described as autonomous, dialogue-driven learning into a semantic network: keyboard input is processed with pattern recognition, stemming, part-of-speech information and Hidden Markov Models, then used to extend the program's database. BOINC distributed the construction of new semantic networks across volunteer computers. Its stated scope was human-like conversational behaviour in English and German, and the project is no longer active.

explainer.example: A user types an English sentence into FreeHAL. The program analyzes its words and patterns, adds information from the exchange to its database, and can use the growing semantic network in later conversation; separately, BOINC volunteers help construct additional networks.

usedIn.name: FreeHAL@home on BOINC
usedIn.detail: Volunteer computing was used to build new semantic networks before the project terminated operations.

explainer.intuition: The central idea was to treat conversation as a way to grow a machine-readable web of knowledge, rather than relying only on a fixed script. Volunteer computers would help expand that web while the chatbot learned from what people typed.
howItWorks: A person communicates with FreeHAL by keyboard in English or German.
The program processes the input using techniques including pattern recognition, stemming, part-of-speech databases and Hidden Markov Models.
Information from the conversation extends FreeHAL's database and semantic network.
The semantic network supports the program's attempt to imitate human conversational behaviour.
Through BOINC, volunteer computers help build new semantic networks for the program.
explainer.whyItMatters: FreeHAL connected two notable ideas: a chatbot that expanded its own knowledge through conversation, and volunteer computing that helped build its semantic networks. Its history also shows how the project evolved from the Java-based JEliza into FreeHAL in May 2008.
misconceptions: FreeHAL was not the HAL computer from 2001: A Space Odyssey; its name was a reference to that film.
It was not Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA, although its original name, JEliza, referred to ELIZA.
It is not an active chatbot service or volunteer-computing project today.
